steps.action:
# The Keeper of Lorn Point

Elias Morrow had been keeping the light for thirty-one years when the storm came that changed everything.

He had come to Lorn Point in the autumn of 1971, a young man with a young man's reasons for wanting to disappear. The lighthouse board had been happy enough to have him — keepers were growing scarce even then, as automation crept along the coastline like a slow tide, replacing human hands with timers and circuitry. Lorn Point was too remote for automation's first wave, set as it was on a finger of black rock that jutted into the North Atlantic three miles from the nearest road. It required a boat to reach in summer and a great deal of faith in winter, when the channel between the rock and the mainland froze in some years and drowned in chop in others.

Elias had grown to love it the way a man loves a difficult marriage — not despite its hardships but because of them. The light required his attention every four hours. The lens required cleaning twice weekly. The generator needed fuel, the walls needed patching, the logbook needed filling with the careful small handwriting he'd developed over the years, precise and vertical as a column of figures. All of this suited him. Busyness was a kind of armor.

What he was armoring himself against, he had never told anyone on the mainland. His supervisor, a squat man named Greer who came by boat every three months with supplies and a cursory inspection, had long since stopped asking personal questions. His daughter, Miriam, wrote letters that arrived in Greer's mail bag and to which Elias responded with care but not intimacy.
